name: id
one_line: print real and effective user and group IDs
plain: `id` tells you who you are to the system: your user number (uid), your main group (gid) and every group you belong to. It is the first command after you land on a machine.
The groups matter: being in sudo, docker, lxd, disk or adm often means an easy path to root.
when: Check who you are after getting a shell.
See whether you belong to sudo, docker or lxd.

examples.title: Who am I?
examples.explain: Prints uid=1000(kali) gid=1000(kali) groups=...; look at the groups list.

examples.title: Another user
examples.explain: Shows that user's ids and groups. Works for any account.

examples.title: Just the user name
examples.explain: -u user id, -n as a name instead of number.

examples.title: Numeric uid only
examples.explain: Useful in scripts: [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ] checks whether you are root.

examples.title: Real versus effective ids
examples.explain: With setuid programs the effective uid can differ from the real uid.

options.plain: Print only the effective user id.
Print only the effective group id.
Print names instead of numbers (with -u, -g or -G).
Print the real id instead of the effective id.

mistakes: Reading only uid and forgetting the groups list.
Assuming uid 0 is the only danger: sudo, docker and lxd groups are almost as good for an attacker.
Confusing id with whoami: whoami prints just the effective user name.
try: Run id, then id root and compare.
Check whether your lab user is in the sudo group.
Write a one-line script that stops if the user is not root.
see_also: whoami(1), groups(1), su(1), sudo(8), getent(1), last(1), w(1).
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
